claims.text: Adding nano-to-micrometer-scale ZrC particles to a TiB2-based or high-entropy boride will improve its resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Ultrasonic mixing will ensure uniform distribution of ZrC particles in the boride powder.
SPS at approximately 2000 °C under an inert atmosphere will densify the composite while preserving uniform ZrC dispersion.
Molten aluminum at approximately 700 °C represents service conditions typical of hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
Conventionally processed unreinforced borides have interconnected grain-boundary networks.
Interconnected grain boundaries in unreinforced borides are prone to molten-aluminum attack and penetration.
ZrC particles will segregate preferentially to boride grain boundaries during sintering.
Grain-boundary ZrC particles will reinforce intergranular regions.
Grain-boundary ZrC particles will reduce the continuity of fast diffusion paths.
ZrC particles will act as physical barriers to molten-aluminum infiltration along boride grain boundaries.
ZrC particles will act as stress concentrators that refine the overall microstructure.
Barrier formation and microstructural refinement will reduce the connectivity of corrosion-prone pathways.
The ZrC-reinforced composite will have a lower corrosion rate than an undoped boride processed under otherwise identical conditions.
The ZrC-reinforced composite will exhibit less mass loss during molten-aluminum exposure than the undoped baseline.
ZrC reinforcement will delay the initiation of molten-aluminum corrosion.
Reduced corrosion will extend the service lifetime of the boride component.
The intervention will remain effective near 700 °C if the ZrC particles remain uniformly distributed and do not significantly agglomerate.
